header.title: Data Engineer | Big Data | Azure | AWS | Databricks

heroTagline: Data Engineering at Scale with AI Augmented Capabilities

resume.short: From Mechatronics Engineering labs to leading AI-augmented data pipeline migrations at one of Brazil's largest banks. The path isn't obvious — and that's precisely the point. Most engineers learn data tools. I started with control theory, physics, and embedded systems, which gave me something most data engineers don't have...
resume.full:
I come from Mechatronics Engineering — calculus, physics, control systems, electronics. That's not a detour from data engineering; it's the foundation for how I think about every system I build: analytically, with attention to constraints, trade-offs, and fundamentals.

I started my career as a Data Engineer Jr building pipelines in a fully on-premises Cloudera environment — PySpark, Hive, Shell scripting, Linux. Getting close to the infrastructure layer built a deep instinct for how data actually moves, and where systems break.

In 2022, everything shifted to Azure and Databricks. I started by helping with migrations and over time I was leading them — pipeline by pipeline, mapping datasets, creating Data Domains, making the architectural decisions that only surface when you move from one paradigm to another. Each migration required optimization, not just translation. To stay grounded in what I was building, I studied cloud architecture intensely and earned multiple certifications along the way. For me, a certification is confirmation I've mastered something, not a badge to collect.

The AI chapter started in 2023 with GitHub Copilot in personal projects. By 2024, it was integrated into my daily workflow at work. In 2025, I was selected for an internal AI pilot program introducing Devin and Windsurf to our team — and was recognized for adapting faster than most. Today I'm leading large-scale migrations of SAS and PowerCenter pipelines to Databricks, applying AI-augmented development at scale — not as a shortcut, but as a force multiplier for engineering judgment.

On the personal side, I build with Claude Code and Codex: multi-agent systems, spec-driven development, context engineering. The reason is simple — I want to understand where this is going, and I want to build things that are genuinely useful to people, while sharpening skills that will matter for years.

A few things that define how I work: I always ask what the trade-offs are between approaches before committing. When a problem feels complex, I break it into parts with clear boundaries, solve each one, and reassemble. I use analogies to make the abstract concrete. If a project requires me to learn something new, I see that as the most interesting part — not a cost.

I believe the engineers who will matter most in the next decade are the ones who understand both the craft and the tools well enough to use one to make the other better. That's the direction I'm moving.

Outside work: I play guitar and sing, read whenever I can, and put my family at the center of everything.

hero.title: dadaia-workspace
hero.tagline: A local-first, spec-driven workspace that gives AI agents current context, a document-governed lifecycle and anti-slop boundaries.

card.summary: Local-first CLI (PyPI): one folder per workspace, six agent harnesses, five agent roles and a document-governed lifecycle from backlog to release.

seo.title: dadaia-workspace — Marco Menezes
seo.description: dadaia-workspace — Python library on PyPI for spec-driven development with collaborative AI agents.

list.diagramAlt: dadaia-workspace architecture diagram: AI agents, project contexts and SDD flow.

sections.title: What is it
sections.body: dadaia-workspace is an open-source CLI (PyPI) for developing with AI agents. A workspace is one folder: your projects live in repos inside it, and the governance (`AGENTS.md`, skills, hooks) sits outside every repo. Work is driven by documents — backlog, SPEC, PLAN and job files — not by a runtime. Five agent roles share them: product engineer, senior and junior software engineer, code reviewer and researcher.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Agents given a whole repository drift: they lose context, write wherever they like and leave their own state behind. dadaia-workspace binds a session to one project, injects only that project's memory and release state, and enforces the boundaries mechanically — a pre-tool gate refuses out-of-scope writes and each refusal carries one fix line.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: `uvx dadaia-workspace init <dir> --harness <name>` creates the workspace and projects the agents into Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, Cursor, Devin or GitHub Copilot. Each task runs in its own git worktree and each job lands only after a reviewer's APPROVED; `worktree pause` and `resume` set a tree aside as a bundle and bring it back. `dadaia export` writes the workspace's contexts to a file (`--hard` adds the unpushed work), and `init --from` rebuilds it elsewhere.

seo.description: Stack, terraform infra, monthly costs, and architectural decisions for marco-menezes.com.

list.diagramAlt: Portfolio infrastructure diagram: S3, CloudFront, Route53, GitHub Actions CI/CD.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: This portfolio is a React SPA hosted on AWS. The frontend is built with Vite and served via CloudFront with OAC over S3. Infrastructure is managed with Terraform and deployment automated via GitHub Actions with OIDC.

sections.title: Engineering
sections.body: Zero long-lived AWS keys: authentication via OIDC directly from GitHub Actions. Two environments (stage + prod) with identical pipelines. Automated tests with Vitest + RTL + Playwright + LHCI before any deployment.

stack.tech: GitHub Actions with OIDC (no long-lived keys)

decisions.title: React/Vite instead of Next.js or Astro
decisions.rationale: High ROI for 5 static routes; no need for SSR or edge rendering.

decisions.title: 2 AWS environments (stage + prod), local dev
decisions.rationale: Explicit gate before prod with no additional cost.

decisions.title: OIDC without long-lived AWS keys
decisions.rationale: No persisted AWS secrets; trust restricted to the portfolio repo.

decisions.title: CMS-lite on the roadmap (not in P0)
decisions.rationale: Future content updates without redeploy, without extra complexity now.

hero.title: rand-engine
hero.tagline: Synthetic data from a declarative spec, for batch and streaming.

media.alt: A terminal runs one Python command. It builds a DataGenerator from a two-column spec, age as an integer from 18 to 80 and plan as free or pro, with seed 42 and 5 rows, and prints a table with the columns age and plan and 5 rows.
media.caption: A spec in, a seeded DataFrame out.

card.summary: Seeded, reproducible DataFrames, related tables, files and event streams from a declarative spec.

seo.title: rand-engine — Marco Menezes
seo.description: rand-engine — open-source Python library on PyPI that generates seeded synthetic data from a declarative spec.

sections.title: Related tables
sections.body: Related tables share the parent's pk spec with the child's fk, so keys stay consistent. Here orders.customer_id is an fk to the customer_id pk of customers.

media.alt: Two tables. The customers table has customer_id, marked pk, and city, with rows 1 Rio, 2 Recife and 3 Rio. The orders table has order_id, marked pk, and customer_id, marked fk, with orders 1, 2 and 3 pointing at customers 2, 1 and 2.
media.caption: orders.customer_id is a foreign key to customers.customer_id. The rows drawn are illustrative.

sections.title: Event streams
sections.body: stream_dict yields an infinite generator of dicts, and the caller stops it. Its event_id is a pk that continues across microbatches, so its values never repeat.

media.alt: A generator built with DataGenerator(spec, seed=1).size(10).stream_dict() emits records one after another, with event_id 1, 2, 3 and 4, each beside a timestamp_created field, and a label says that it never ends.
media.caption: Each record carries the next event_id, and the stream never ends.

sections.title: Files in parts
sections.body: Writing with numFiles above 1 saves a folder of part files instead of one file. The pk values never repeat between parts.

media.alt: A terminal runs one Python command that writes 1000 rows of a pk column named id to a CSV file with numFiles set to 3. A second command lists the output folder, which holds three files named part_, an id and .csv.
media.caption: One save, three part files.

sections.title: Try it
sections.code:
from rand_engine import DataGenerator

spec = {
    "user_id": {"method": "int_zfilled", "kwargs": {"length": 8}},
    "age": {"method": "integers", "kwargs": {"min": 18, "max": 80}},
    "plan": {"method": "distincts_prop", "kwargs": {"distincts": {"free": 8, "pro": 2}}},
    "signup": {"method": "dates", "kwargs": {"start": "2024-01-01", "end": "2024-12-31"}},
}

df = DataGenerator(spec, seed=42).size(1_000).get_df()
print(df.head())

sections.title: Why use it
sections.body: Pipelines need test data, with nulls and anomalies on demand. Related tables keep their pk and fk keys consistent across batches, streams and files.
